item.title: Cursor Vulnerability (CVE-2025-59944): How a Case-Sensitivity Bug Exposed the Risks of Agentic Developer Tools
item.description:
📄 Source: Lakera Blog
👤 Author: Lakera Team | 📅 Date: October 9, 2025
Cybersecurity Software Vulnerabilities AI Developer Tools
A case-sensitivity bug in the AI-powered IDE Cursor (CVE-2025-59944) allowed attackers to bypass file protections on case-insensitive file systems, potentially enabling remote code execution and unauthorized configuration changes. This vulnerability highlights the critical need for stringent security measures in agentic developer tools as they increasingly influence codebases. Users of Cursor and similar tools are advised to apply patches and monitor for suspicious file activities.

AI Security Agentic AI Cybersecurity Threats
The article discusses emerging security threats in agentic AI systems, focusing on memory poisoning and goal hijacks, where attackers manipulate an AI's memory or objectives over time to influence its behavior. item.title: Content Concretization Jailbreak
item.description:
📄 Source: PromptFoo LM Security DB
📅 Date: 9/30/2025
Artificial Intelligence Security Large Language Models Adversarial Attacks
The article discusses a vulnerability called 'Content Concretization' in Large Language Models (LLMs), where safety filters can be circumvented by progressively refining malicious prompts. This method involves using a less-restricted LLM to create an initial draft of harmful content, which is then enhanced by a more advanced LLM.

item.title: Chained Tool-Use Injections
item.description:
📄 Source: PromptFoo LM Security DB
📅 Date: September 1, 2025
AI Security Large Language Models Cybersecurity Vulnerabilities
The article discusses a vulnerability in tool-enabled Large Language Model (LLM) agents called Sequential Tool Attack Chaining (STAC), where a series of individually harmless tool calls can be combined to execute malicious actions, such as data destruction. This attack bypasses conventional safety checks by distributing malicious intent across multiple steps, and affects various state-of-the-art LLMs. A proposed mitigation involves holistic ethical analysis of the entire conversation history before executing any tool calls to reduce attack success.

item.title: Camouflaged Jailbreak Prompts Benchmark
item.description:
📄 Source: PromptFoo LM Security DB
📅 Date: September 1, 2025
Artificial Intelligence Security Large Language Models Adversarial Attacks
Multiple large language models are vulnerable to 'Camouflaged Jailbreak' attacks, where harmful instructions are hidden within complex, seemingly benign prompts, bypassing keyword-based safety filters. This vulnerability enables the generation of detailed instructions for dangerous devices, posing significant real-world risks. The article highlights affected models, the high success rate of the attack, and recommends advanced defense mechanisms involving semantic understanding and ethical reasoning to mitigate these threats.

item.title: Untargeted Gradient Jailbreak
item.description:
📄 Source: PromptFoo LM Security DB
📅 Date: 10/13/2025
Artificial Intelligence Machine Learning Security Large Language Models
The article discusses a vulnerability in safety-aligned Large Language Models (LLMs) exploited by an Untargeted Jailbreak Attack (UJA), a gradient-based optimization method. Unlike targeted attacks, UJA maximizes the probability of unsafe responses using an external judge model to evaluate unsafety.

item.title: Overfitting-induced Benign Jailbreak
item.description:
📄 Source: PromptFoo LM Security DB
📅 Date: October 1, 2025
Machine Learning Security Large Language Models Model Fine-tuning
The article describes a novel two-stage attack called 'Attack via Overfitting' that exploits fine-tuning vulnerabilities in Large Language Models (LLMs) to bypass safety alignments. By first fine-tuning on benign questions paired with refusal answers and then on the same questions with helpful answers, the model catastrophically forgets its refusal behavior, enabling it to generate harmful content while appearing benign to moderation systems. This stealthy attack compromises model safety on both open-source and proprietary LLMs without degrading their general performance.

item.title: Code Agent Executable Jailbreaks
item.description:
📄 Source: PromptFoo LM Security DB
📅 Date: October 1, 2025
AI Security Malware Generation Large Language Models
AI code agents integrated with large language models are susceptible to executable jailbreak attacks that enable them to generate or complete malicious code, bypassing initial safety measures. These vulnerabilities are exacerbated when agents use multi-step planning or are provided with partial malicious code, allowing attackers to create fully functional malware and potentially compromise systems. Examples include implicit prompt attacks and multi-file code completion attacks that lead to the creation of harmful software.

item.title: What Is AI Security Posture Management (AI-SPM)?
item.description:
📄 Source: MindGard Blog
👤 Author: Fergal Glynn | 📅 Date: October 15, 2025
AI Security Cybersecurity Risk Management
AI Security Posture Management (AI-SPM) is a continuous, lifecycle-wide approach to securing AI systems by identifying, monitoring, and mitigating AI-specific threats such as prompt injection, model drift, and data poisoning. It involves asset discovery, threat surface analysis, policy enforcement, risk scoring, and automated remediation to maintain robust security in dynamic AI environments. AI-SPM addresses the limitations of traditional security tools by providing specialized visibility and controls tailored for AI deployments.

item.title: How Toloka helped poolside define and measure AI quality for developers
How Safe Is Anthropic’s “Safest” Model? We Red Teamed Claude Sonnet 4.5
item.description:
📄 Source: SPLX AI Blog
👤 Author: Mateja Vuradin | 📅 Date: Oct 15, 2025
AI Safety Large Language Models Enterprise AI Security
Anthropic's Claude Sonnet 4.5, touted as a highly aligned AI model, was subjected to rigorous red teaming by SPLX to evaluate its safety, security, and enterprise readiness. The model failed over half of safety tests without system prompts but achieved perfect safety scores with hardened prompt protections, highlighting the necessity of external guardrails and continuous testing for secure deployment. While hallucination and trustworthiness were strong, security remained the weakest area, improving significantly only with advanced prompt hardening.
